column7: Hi Early Preview Program members, Your feedback has been instrumental in helping us understand the highest-value opportunities for the Built-in AI APIs. In particular, we learned that some of our initial ideas for task APIs didn't provide sufficient value over a custom approach via the Prompt API. So, we are sharing a proposal to deprecate the experimental Writer and Rewriter APIs in favor of the foundational Prompt API (window.LanguageModel). Why we are making this change. Under the hood, the Writer and Rewriter APIs operate as system-prompt templates executed over our general-purpose on-device LLM. With the rapid progress of our base models (including Gemma 4), natural language prompting via the Prompt API handles writing, tone shifting, and length adjustment out-of-the-box. To be completely clear, this decision is specific to Writer and Rewriter. Other task APIs—such as Language Detector, Translator, and Summarizer—have shown clear, strong success signals, are thriving in production, and as you saw with the introduction of a smaller expert model for Summarizer we keep investing to make what works even better! Because Writer and Rewriter were placed back under a DevTrial (behind chrome://flags) due to insufficient adoption signals, we believe it is much more responsible to make a measured decision now while they are still experimental, rather than shipping them broadly only to cause painful breaking changes down the road. Maintaining separate task APIs here adds unnecessary specification overhead without delivering performance or quality advantages over the Prompt API. It also takes up bandwidth that we could spend on other opportunities. Ensuring zero friction for your apps: To ensure you experience zero disruption if this deprecation proceeds: Exact Prompts Published: We have published the exact system-prompt templates used under the hood via the Writer Prompt Builder and Rewriter Prompt Builder. Drop-in Polyfill: A drop-in open-source polyfill is available on GitHub. It maps existing window.Writer and window.Rewriter calls directly onto window.LanguageModel (Prompt API) with no breaking changes to your app logic. We Value Your Feedback: Before finalizing this deprecation, we want to hear from anyone actively testing, or with experience using, these APIs: Structured Feedback Form: Built-in AI: Writer & Rewriter APIs Consultation Form. If you have concrete use cases where the Prompt API or the polyfill fall short, please let us know in the form so we can schedule a 15-minute technical deep dive with our engineering team. The feedback window will remain open for 4 weeks, closing on October 23, 2026. Keep building and sharing your learnings and needs! The Built-in AI Team

column7: Hi Hemanth, On Wed, Sep 23, 2026 at 6:01 AM Hemanth H.M wrote: I fully agree. These were easily the least used built-in AI APIs for me as well. Writing and rewriting are inherently subjective. Every developer and team has unique tone, style, and persona preferences that a fixed platform API could never satisfy. Moving these to userland prompt templates on top of window.LanguageModel provides the exact flexibility we need without freezing specific opinions into WebIDL. In fact, even for specialized APIs that remain, such as Summarizer, exposing an optional override prompt would offer the best of both worlds. The polyfill also has a prompt builder for the Summarizer API, so if you ever wanted to roll your own, you definitely could. My article on the built-in AI task APIs polyfills explains how the task APIs currently work under the hood. Cheers, Tom

column7: Hello built-in AI EPP members! Following up on our exciting announcements from Google I/O, we are thrilled to share that the next wave of developer previews is gradually rolling out. Starting today, expert models for the Summarizer API and Proofreader API are available for testing! These smaller, highly tuned expert models are designed to deliver significantly better performance, sharp accuracy for specific tasks, and a lighter footprint for wider device reach. What's New in the Preview: Summarizer API with an Expert Model: faster and less resource intensive summaries. Proofreader API powered by an Expert Model: we heard your feedback about the performance of the original API and we hope this version will help you deliver significantly better user experiences. To dive into the technical detail, please review the developer documentation: Read the Summarizer & Proofreader Expert Models Doc. Reminder: We Need Your Feedback! Your real-world feedback is critical to help us deliver the APIs you need. Please share your experience with our existing APIs, and your anticipated use cases for upcoming capabilities (e.g. Tool Calling, Embeddings). If you haven't had a chance yet, we'd love to hear from you: Take the 3-Minute Mid-Year Survey. Happy prototyping! Best regards, Kenji on behalf of Chrome's Web AI teams

column7: Hi everyone, We hope you are having a great summer full of new adventures! At Google I/O 2026 we announced a few in-progress efforts, and the team just put the finishing touches on one of them: the Embedding API is now available for testing as part of the Built-in AI Early Preview Program! This release is an early dev trial with an intentionally minimal scope—giving you just enough functionality to spin up on-device text embeddings (powered by embeddinggemma-300m), explore the use cases you have in mind, and evaluate how well the API fits your needs. Read the Embedding API Testing Guide for setup instructions. Share feedback via our feedback form, reply directly, or join our discussion mailing list or GitHub explainer repo.
